Collect angles from reviews, comments and sales calls.

textLines: Why your Google Ads account needs fewer campaigns, not more
Most accounts we audit have between 40 and 120 campaigns. Most of them would make more money with eight.
Every new campaign splits your budget and your data. Google's bidding needs volume to learn, and a small campaign never gets enough of it. The result is higher costs and reports nobody can read.
When we audited Oakline last year they had 64 search campaigns. Thirty of them spent less than £20 a day. None of those thirty had enough conversions for smart bidding to work.
We group by intent and margin, not by product line. One campaign for people ready to buy, one for people comparing, one for brand. Everything else is a test with an end date.
"We stopped asking which campaign to add and started asking which one to switch off." Our four step rebuild
Export every search term from the last 12 months.
Group terms by intent and by gross margin.
Rebuild into no more than ten campaigns.
Review weekly and kill anything without a clear job.
Our team mapping search intent for a B2B client.
Within eight weeks Oakline's cost per demo fell 38% and their weekly report shrank from four pages to one. The account is easier to run, and the bidding finally has enough data to work.

textLines: TikTok for B2B: what worked in our last 12 tests
B2B on TikTok sounds like a stretch. Across twelve tests for SaaS and services clients, three formats consistently produced pipeline.
We ran every test with the same budget, the same audience rules and the same goal: booked demos, not views.
Short, unpolished videos where a founder explains one problem outperformed every produced ad. People trusted the person more than the brand.
Real customers describing the before and after drove the cheapest demo bookings. We kept them under thirty seconds and added captions for silent viewing.
"Nobody on TikTok wants an ad. They will happily watch someone solve a problem." How we ran the tests
One format per test, nothing else changed.
Two weeks per test at a fixed daily budget.
Success measured on demos, not clicks.
Winners rerun with new hooks to confirm.
Polished brand videos and generic product demos struggled to hold attention past three seconds. Anything that looked like an ad was treated like one.

textLines: How to build a topic map that ranks for buying intent
A topic map is a plan for which questions you will answer and in what order. Done well, it turns content into a sales channel.
Most content plans start with keyword volume. Ours start with the product, because that is where the revenue is.
List every product and the questions people ask before buying it. Those questions are your first articles, and they usually have far less competition than broad terms.
We rank each topic by how close it sits to a purchase and how hard it will be to rank. High intent, low effort topics go first.
"Traffic that never buys is just a bigger server bill." Write for the buyer
Answer the question in the first paragraph.
Show the product where it genuinely helps.
Add one clear next step at the end.
Refresh the page every six months.
Every article links to the product it supports and to two related guides, so authority flows to the pages where revenue happens.

textLines: How to edit this template, from the CMS to colors, fonts, forms and interactions.
Tidemark uses Client-First class naming, components for the Navbar, Footer and CTA, and Variables for every repeated value. This guide covers what to edit after you duplicate the template.

Five CMS collections power the dynamic pages: Blog Posts, Case Studies, Jobs, Services and Team Members. Open the CMS panel to add, edit or remove items. Each template page takes its SEO title and meta description from the item, so new items need no extra setup.
To feature a blog post at the top of the Blog page, switch on its Featured field. Only one featured post shows at a time.
Every color, font size, spacing value and radius is a Variable. Open the Variables panel to change a value once and update it across the whole site.

The Base collection holds the brand colors. The Color Scheme collection has Base, Dark and Brand modes for sections. Typography and Spacing have Tablet and Mobile modes, so sizes scale down on smaller screens.

Tidemark uses Geist, licensed under the SIL Open Font License 1.1. To use another font, add it in Site settings under Fonts, then select it on the Body (All Pages) tag and the heading tags in the Style panel.

All animations are built with Webflow Interactions in the Designer, with no custom JavaScript. Open the Interactions panel to edit the scroll reveals, the testimonial switcher, the FAQ accordions and the table of contents highlight on the legal pages.

The contact, job application and newsletter forms are native Webflow forms with custom success and error messages. Submissions are sent to the email address in Site settings under Forms. Change it to your own address before you publish.
All images are WebP files under 150 KB, stored in this project. To swap one, select the image and choose a new file in its settings, then write alt text that describes what it shows.

The only custom code is a noindex meta tag in the head of the Privacy, Terms, Style Guide, Licenses, Changelog and Instructions pages, so search engines skip them. You can find it in Page settings under Custom code. Remove it if you want one of these pages indexed.
Font, image and icon licenses are listed on the Licenses page. For help with this template, email hello@fluxory.studio.
